content.content:
`deccy record --from <handle> --to <node> [path...]` lands one open draft: it records into that node's change the changed paths of the union of the target change's current owned set and the ref paths the draft's node document adds, and, inside that same recording, turns the draft's record `landed`. It is the recording the verb already is — `deccy record <path>... --to <id>` places the named file edits into the named node's change — reached through a different selection of the edits, not through a second verb, a second landing or a second operation (rvyrosmp, qvkuluyw). `--to` stays required in both forms and still names the one node whose change receives the edits; the recording still creates no node and no change, draws no edge, and lands nothing outside an owning change (rvyrosmp). What `--from` adds is a source — one draft, addressed by its handle — and the refusals that exist only because there is a source to test; it removes nothing the path form already required, and it makes `record` neither creation nor removal (rvyrosmp).

`--from <handle>` names the draft by the only value that picks a record out, its handle, and the record is read as the one JSON document at `.deccy/work/<handle>.json` whose filename is that handle; no index beside the documents and no search for "the draft of this node" supplies the source (twpvqstu, owyntkvw). A handle the directory does not name is a record that is not there, and the invocation is refused with nothing placed. A source form that found a draft from its node, its edit or its workspace would address the registry through references that are many per record, and would give one draft a second key; the landing therefore takes the handle and reads the document the handle names, and the state it later writes goes into that same document (twpvqstu, owyntkvw). The record names exactly one node, exactly one edit and exactly one workspace, and a draft names exactly one node (owyntkvw, znskspqs); so one source is one draft, and a landing names exactly one draft even when several drafts name the same node.

The `--to` must be the node the record names. Because the record names exactly one node (owyntkvw), the draft names exactly one node (znskspqs) and `--to` names the one change the edits would enter (rvyrosmp), the landing either agrees them or refuses: a `--to` naming another node refuses and places nothing, and so does an invocation that names no `--to` at all, `--to` being required in both forms (rvyrosmp). The source never re-points the draft to the node the caller named, never records into a node the record does not name, and never reads `--to` as overriding the record; the node is the record's reference and `--to` is the surface the agreement is tested on. Nor is there a second receiving change in the call: the landing creates no new `nodes/` document and attributes no record to a change; the one `nodes/` document it writes is the draft's node document, and the only content that moves is the content of the one change `--to` names (owyntkvw, rvyrosmp).

A source that is the target change is refused. The node `--to` names is a change id: a node's id is the id of the jj change that owns it, appearing in the node's filename and in edge targets and never as document content (xwyryumr). When the source's references — the edit and the workspace the record names (owyntkvw) — resolve to that same change, the recording is refused and nothing is placed, because the edits a landing would move are already that change's content and the recording would be the change into itself. The comparison is between change ids and only change ids: the node id is the owning jj change id (xwyryumr), and a refusal resting on a commit id, on a workspace's name or path, or on a record handle would be a different test — a commit id is not the node's identity, a workspace is a reference the record carries and not the change, and a handle names a record and never a change (xwyryumr, owyntkvw). Which of the record's references is the one that reaches the change is not fixed here; what is fixed is that the identity compared is the owning change id.

The landable set is the union of two sources, neither narrowing the other: the target change's current owned set, and the ref paths the draft's node document adds. The first source is the set the target change owns now — its node document plus the repo-relative paths its `content.ref` lists when that field is an array, or the node document alone when it is inline (xzxtxymq) — read at the change that owns the node as qrqsxyzz reads it. The second source is the draft's node document, read from the draft's own workspace, where that draft's edits live (znskspqs): writing that document into the target's change makes owned every ref path it lists that the target change did not already own, and a ref path newly listed there is a changed path of the union, placed in the same recording. A path the landing places must be owned by the target change either before the recording — in its current owned set — or through the node document the recording writes; no path outside that union is placed, so not the other paths of the draft's workspace, not the other paths of the target change, and not a working copy's dirty set read as a source of ownership. Every changed path of the union is placed by the one landing the draft has: one recording carries both sources' changed paths, because the draft has no second landing in which a leftover could be placed (vkkwusty, xzxtxymq). A ref path the draft's node document drops stays in the union through the target's current owned set: if the draft carries a deletion for it, the deletion is placed, and if the draft leaves the file as the target change already holds it, it is simply unchanged. Within the union a path is changed when the content the draft carries for it differs from the content the target change holds for it; the encoding of that comparison, and whether it is taken once or path by path, is not fixed here (xzxtxymq). A draft whose union content is unchanged has no changed union path and no landing: the invocation refuses and the record stays `open`, because a landing is the recording of a draft's edits and there is nothing to record. That is not zxrrwrky's rule extended to the source form; it is the landing having nothing to place.

The `[path...]` arguments are optional, and they are optional only in this form. `deccy record --to <id>` naming no path refuses the invocation and places nothing (zxrrwrky): that form names the edits it places by path, so an invocation naming none cannot do what it says. A source form names the edits otherwise — the draft and the union name them — so it does not need the caller to name them again, and path-optionality attaches to the form that already names its edits elsewhere, never to `record` as a verb: `deccy record --to <id>` still refuses, and a source form that omitted `--to` still refuses, because `--to` is the one part both forms require (zxrrwrky, rvyrosmp). When the source form is given paths they state the changed union instead of replacing it: every named path is in the union and changed, every changed union path is named, and a disagreement refuses with nothing placed. A named subset is not a landing of part of a draft — a draft lands as a whole, and its record has nowhere to go afterwards but `landed` (znskspqs, vkkwusty) — and a named path outside the union would land an edit neither the target's current owned set nor the written document makes owned (xzxtxymq, rvyrosmp). The arguments therefore let a caller state the set it expects and be refused when the draft says otherwise; they never select a partial landing, and they never license a path the union does not hold.

A stale draft refuses the landing, on qrqsxyzz's terms and not re-decided here. That node fixes the comparison — a content-identity base of the node's owned set taken at the opening, compared path by path against the owned set as it stands at landing, both sides read at the change that owns the node (qrqsxyzz). The set that comparison reads is the target's current owned set as that node fixes it, not the union this recording places from and not the paths a call names: a ref path the draft's node document newly lists becomes owned through the landing's own write, so it is a change for the landing to place rather than a difference that makes a draft stale (qrqsxyzz, xzxtxymq). What this node adds is only that the landing is a recording that comparison applies to, and that it lands under the rule as that node states it, which holds for each record naming the node: an open record naming the target node that is stale refuses the landing even when the source is a different, current record, and the refusal names each stale handle with the paths that differ for it (qrqsxyzz). A landing that skipped the check, or that placed the edits and refused afterwards, would contradict it (qrqsxyzz).

Only an open draft lands, and landing is per draft. A record has exactly two states, `open` and `landed`, the only transition is `open` → `landed`, and a landed record is retained rather than deleted (vkkwusty). A source naming a record whose state is `landed` therefore refuses and changes nothing: there is no transition out of `landed`, no reopening for a redraft, and no second landing for that draft — a redraft is a new draft and a new record (vkkwusty). Because a node may carry several drafts and each draft is recorded into its own node as its own operation (znskspqs), landing one draft leaves every other draft naming the same node exactly as it was: still open, still carrying its own base, untouched by this recording.

The state write rides inside the recording. The record is one JSON document and its state is a field of that document (twpvqstu), so landing writes `landed` into the document it read the draft from and then keeps it (vkkwusty, twpvqstu). That write is partial work inside the recording the verb already is, not an operation of its own: it is not bracketed apart, not a fourth member of the operation vocabulary, and not a second landing beside the one the caller asked for (qvkuluyw). Placing the changed union paths and marking the record are one landing; their internal order, and where between answering the argument surface and writing anything the reads are taken, are not fixed here (qvkuluyw, qrqsxyzz).

Every refusal above is the precondition of that same recording, so a refused landing places nothing: no changed union path is moved into any change, no record's state is written, no node or change is created, and nothing of the graph changes (rvyrosmp, qvkuluyw). A landing that placed some paths and refused the rest would be two outcomes of one recording; the recording either holds and does both of its parts, the placement and the `landed` write, or is refused and does neither. The order in which the refusals are tested, and which one a caller meets first when several hold, is not fixed here.

Deliberately not here. The exact wording, separators, ordering, stream and exit status of any refusal are not fixed, only that a refusal places nothing and that a stale-draft refusal names the handle and the differing paths (qrqsxyzz). Also not fixed: how a handle is generated or a draft opened, the source arriving with a handle already minted (owyntkvw, twpvqstu); how the record's references resolve to a jj change (xwyryumr); the encoding of the content comparison that finds the changed union paths (xzxtxymq); what a stale draft may then do; the surface that lists drafts; any cap on open records or barrier over them; the marker stack and which change is trunk; and every verb other than `record`. Each of those can change without touching what is settled here: one source form on the recording the verb already is, the target agreed with the record's node by owning change id, the changed union paths and no others, the path-only refusal intact, and the `landed` write inside that same recording.
content.rationale:
This decision cashes a draft model the graph already fixed: a draft names exactly one node and the edit it belongs to, is written in its own workspace, a node may carry several drafts, and landing is per draft (znskspqs). The draft's record already had an identity and references (owyntkvw), a storage location and a way of being found (twpvqstu), a lifecycle (vkkwusty), and a place inside the operation vocabulary (qvkuluyw), and the landing already existed as a recording that compares the owned set before it places anything (rvyrosmp, qrqsxyzz). What was missing is the surface that lands a named draft, and the whole design question is whether that surface is a new verb. It is not, and every choice here follows from refusing to make it one.

The landing is the recording it already is (qvkuluyw). `record <path>... --to <id>` places the named edits into the named node's change, `--to` is required, it creates no node, and nothing lands outside an owning change (rvyrosmp); a landing is exactly such a recording, so the only thing a source form may vary is how the edits are selected. That is why `--to` stays required and still names the one receiving change, why no node or edge is created, and why the `landed` write is placed inside the recording rather than beside it: if it were an operation of its own the registry would have entered the operation vocabulary through the one door that vocabulary closes, and undo would have to step the placement and the state write separately (qvkuluyw). Making the write partial work inside the recording is the only shape in which a landing is one operation and the record still turns.

The source is addressed by the handle because the handle is the one thing that picks a record out, and the record is the one document at `.deccy/work/<handle>.json` (owyntkvw, twpvqstu). A landing that found its draft from a node, an edit or a workspace would use references the record itself calls many-per-record, and would make the filename follow something other than the key; reading the handle-named document keeps the registry's identity and its discovery intact and gives the landing one draft rather than a candidate set.

`--to` must agree with the record's node because the record names exactly one node and a draft names exactly one node (owyntkvw, znskspqs), while `--to` names the one change the edits enter (rvyrosmp). Three prerequisites already say which node is involved, so a landing cannot choose: a `--to` naming another node, or none, refuses and places nothing, rather than re-pointing the draft or writing into the caller's node. Refusing is the only outcome that keeps the record's reference and the receiving change the same node.

The source-that-is-the-target refusal is the identity rule applied, not a second rule. A node's id is the owning jj change id and never a commit id, and it names the node in its filename and in edge targets (xwyryumr); the record's workspace and edit are references and the handle is a key (owyntkvw). So the test is between change ids: a source resolving to the change `--to` names would record that change into itself, and a test resting on a commit id, a workspace path or a handle would be testing something the node model says is not the node's identity. Refusing keeps the recording from becoming a no-op that still turns a record landed.

The recorded paths are the changed paths of a union because ownership is exact (xzxtxymq), and the union has two sources neither of which narrows the other. The first is the target change's current owned set — its node document plus the ref paths its `content.ref` already lists, or the node document alone when inline — read at the change that owns the node, which is the same set qrqsxyzz fixes for staleness. The second is the draft's node document, read from the draft's own workspace, where the draft's edits live (znskspqs); writing that document into the target change makes owned the ref paths it adds, so their edits belong to the same recording. A path the landing places is owned either before the recording, in the current owned set, or through the document the recording writes; nothing outside the union is placed, so the workspace's other files, the change's other tree and a dirty working copy stay out, which is the custody rule the recording guard checks. Taking the set from either source alone is the defect the union fixes: from the current document alone, a ref the draft adds is changed content the recording makes owned and does not place; from the draft's document alone, a ref the draft drops is excluded even though the target change still owns it and may carry a deletion to place. In the union both are placeable in the one recording the draft has, and every changed path of the union is placed by it, because the draft has no second landing in which a leftover could be placed (vkkwusty, xzxtxymq). A ref the draft drops stays in the union through the current owned set: a deletion the draft carries is placed, and a file the draft leaves exactly as the target holds it is unchanged. The stale comparison does not move with the union: it reads the target's current owned set at the change that owns the node, as qrqsxyzz fixes it, so a ref the draft adds is a change to place, not a staleness difference, and the union neither widens nor narrows what staleness reads. The owner is also why the `[path...]` arguments cannot be a selection that widens or narrows the landing: a subset would leave part of a draft unrecorded while its record is already terminal, since a landed record has no way back (vkkwusty) and landing is per draft (znskspqs), and a superset would place an edit the union does not hold (xzxtxymq, rvyrosmp). What the arguments can honestly do is state the changed union and be refused when the draft says otherwise, which is a guard on the caller rather than a licence to the landing.

Path-optionality is scoped to this form and only this form. `deccy record --to <id>` naming no path refuses and places nothing (zxrrwrky), because the form names its edits by path and an invocation naming none cannot do what it promises. A source form names its edits through the draft and the union, so the caller need not name them again — but that is a property of the source form, not a relaxation of `record`: the path-only invocation keeps its refusal, and `--to` stays required in both forms (zxrrwrky, rvyrosmp). Any other reading would make the empty path-only invocation legal, which the recorded requirement forbids.

Staleness is referenced, not re-decided. qrqsxyzz fixes the base, the comparison over the whole owned set, the read at the owning change, the refusal, and the naming of the differing paths; this node only says that the landing is a recording that comparison applies to, and takes the rule as stated, including that it holds for each record naming the node (qrqsxyzz). The set stays the target's current owned set as that node fixes it, not the union the landing places from: a ref path the draft's node document adds becomes owned only through the landing's own write, so it is a change for the landing to place rather than a difference that makes the draft stale. A stale draft that is not the source can therefore refuse a landing, which is exactly what that requirement says and what keeps one draft's edits from landing against content another open draft was opened on.

Only an open draft lands because a record has exactly two states and one direction, and the landed record is retained (vkkwusty). No transition out of `landed` means no second landing and no reopening; a redraft arrives as a new record. Landing per draft (znskspqs) means the other drafts naming the same node are untouched, which is what makes alternatives and redrafts coexist rather than queue.

What is left out is left out because it is decidable elsewhere without touching these clauses: the wording and exit status of a refusal, the order refusals are tested in, how a handle is minted or a draft opened (owyntkvw, twpvqstu), how references resolve to a change (xwyryumr), the encoding of the content comparison (xzxtxymq), repair for a stale draft, the drafts listing surface, the cap and barrier, and the marker stack. Each belongs to a commitment the graph places elsewhere; fixing them here would freeze details a reader cannot check against the record and would make this node answer questions no prerequisite asks.
